projects.name: Finding intent in the conversation
projects.summary: An LLM-powered system that finds buying and selling signals in communication streams, then alerts the agent when a prospect needs help.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: A prospect’s next move can be buried in an ordinary reply. Real estate teams need a way to notice those signals across newsletters, drip campaigns, and ongoing conversations.

sections.title: What I built
paragraphs: The system ingests communication streams and uses LLM reasoning to extract explicit and implicit buying or selling intent. It sends real-time alerts to agents when a prospect needs assistance.
This is the current main product at Clarity Works. It brings together the work I enjoy most: understanding the operational problem and translating it into a working AI pipeline.

sections.title: Where it stands
paragraphs: The product is live in pilot testing. I’m keeping that distinction clear: a deployed pilot is an important step, and its broader business impact still needs to be measured.

sections.title: The design question
paragraphs: How do you distinguish a useful signal from a plausible interpretation? For an intent system, that question matters as much as the extraction itself. It is the part of the work I want to make visible as the pilot develops.

projects.name: A small team’s outbound engine
projects.summary: Seven stages, three LLM agents, and deterministic checks around the work. Personalized outreach grew from about 10 to 60+ messages per day.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: As a solo founder, researching accounts and writing relevant first messages competed with the time needed to build and deliver. I wanted more throughput while preserving account-specific context.

sections.title: What I built
paragraphs: I built a seven-stage Python pipeline covering lead scraping, enrichment, routing, personalized drafting, and upload to Instantly. Three LLM agents handle enrichment, routing, and drafting, calling Claude through OpenRouter. Apify and Google Sheets connect the research and operating workflow.
The cold-email infrastructure is part of this system: the value comes from connecting those stages into an end-to-end process.

sections.title: The checks around the model
paragraphs: Do-not-contact checks run at three stages. Email verification happens before sending, a cross-channel reply-stop prevents continued follow-up, and a human approval gate sits before messages ship. These controls live in the workflow and code.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: Personalized outreach increased from roughly 10 to more than 60 messages per day. That is a throughput result from my own operation; it is not a claim about response rates or revenue.

projects.name: Closing the lead-to-response gap
projects.summary: A B2B SaaS that sends automated SMS alerts for inbound real estate leads within five minutes, with failover logic.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: An inbound lead is only useful if someone notices it in time. LeadPulse focused on the handoff between a new enquiry and the agent who needs to respond.

sections.title: What I built
paragraphs: I built and shipped a B2B SaaS providing automated SMS lead alerts within five minutes, with failover logic. The system was designed around a clear operational action: get the lead in front of an agent.

sections.title: Beyond the happy path
paragraphs: Shipping included navigating Twilio A2P 10DLC registration and CASL requirements. Messaging infrastructure and the practical conditions for operating it were part of the product work.

sections.title: What this work demonstrates
paragraphs: A bounded product with a concrete user, a time-sensitive workflow, and delivery concerns beyond the UI. I’m describing the shipped capability here; adoption and conversion results are not yet part of the public case study.

projects.name: The content engine behind Clarity Works
projects.summary: A documented, seven-stage AI-assisted production line that connects one recording to published video, learning material, and repurposed content.
projects.outcome: Under 2 hours on a six-minute video

sections.title: The operational problem
paragraphs: Content was valuable, repeatable work with too many handoffs held in one person’s memory. As a solo founder, I needed a production process I could run consistently alongside the business.

sections.title: The production line
paragraphs: I documented seven gated stages, with a finished deliverable moving into the next step. A shared knowledge base keeps the output aligned with the business. Claude, Descript, and ElevenLabs support the work; recording and editorial judgment stay with me.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: The published proof asset reports moving from a 5+ hour manual baseline to under two hours from raw idea to upload for a six-minute video. It also records 16 published videos at the time that example was captured.

sections.title: More than one output
paragraphs: The same recording supports YouTube and the Sprint pre-watch library, with a repurposing stage for other channels. The full walkthrough is public, so the workflow can be inspected alongside the claim.

projects.name: Building AI capability that stays with the team
projects.summary: A workflow-first advisory method: understand the business, diagnose the work, improve the SOP, then build with the team.
projects.outcome: A structured method, teaching assets, and handoff

sections.title: The problem I work on
paragraphs: New tools do not resolve an unclear process. I started Clarity Works around a practical question: how can a non-technical team learn to improve its own work with AI?

sections.title: The method
paragraphs: The operating sequence is context, diagnosis, SOP, and build. I use it to turn business goals and scattered tasks into a clear workflow, then help the team build the AI-assisted version. Capability transfer runs through the engagement.

sections.title: How I package it
paragraphs: The 30-day Sprint is designed around one improved SOP, one useful workflow, and a roadmap for the next opportunities. The phased Partner Program extends the method across core operations, with documentation, ownership, and review habits. These are the programs’ intended deliverables.

sections.title: Teaching in the open
paragraphs: I publish the frameworks on YouTube and use those materials as pre-work. Live sessions can then focus on the client’s actual process, decisions, and build.

notes.title: The SOP is part of the architecture
notes.summary: Before choosing the agent, understand the decisions, handoffs, and exceptions in the work.
paragraphs: When a team asks for an AI workflow, my first question is about the work itself. What starts it? Who makes the decision? What information do they need? Where does the process stall?

Those questions are architectural. A model can help interpret an input, but the surrounding workflow still needs clear ownership, inputs, outputs, and a useful next action. An undocumented process makes those decisions harder to see.

That is why workflow mapping and SOP improvement come before the assisted build in the AI Capability Ladder I use at Clarity Works. The process gives the build its shape. It also gives the team something concrete to question and improve.

I want a working session to leave behind more than a promising demo. The team should be able to explain what the workflow does, recognize when it needs human judgment, and maintain the process as the work changes.
For me, discovery and engineering belong in the same conversation. Understanding the process is how I decide what is worth building.

notes.title: Build the checks around the model
notes.summary: What my outbound pipeline taught me about putting operational rules in code.
paragraphs: My outbound pipeline uses three LLM agents for enrichment, routing, and drafting. Those are useful places for contextual reasoning. The operating rules around them need a different treatment.

A do-not-contact record needs to stop the workflow. A reply needs to stop follow-up. An unverified email needs to be checked before sending. These rules should be explicit in the system that runs the work.

In the pipeline, do-not-contact checks run at three stages, verification happens before send, and a cross-channel reply-stop prevents continued follow-up. There is also a human approval gate before a message ships.
The distinction shapes how I think about applied AI: use the model where interpretation helps, and make the boundaries around its output inspectable. A well-written prompt is one part of that design.

The result I can point to today is throughput: personalized outreach grew from about ten to more than sixty messages a day. To tell the full business story, response quality and downstream outcomes need their own measurement.

hero_description: I’m Vatsal — a founder, builder, and advisor. I turn operational problems into useful AI workflows, then help the people doing the work understand and own them.

about.lead: My economics background made me curious about incentives and ownership. Building AI systems made that practical.
paragraphs: I founded Clarity Works to help service-based businesses build AI capability inside their teams. I work from business context to workflow diagnosis, SOP improvement, and the first useful AI-assisted build.

That same method shapes my own systems: an outbound engine, an intent-extraction pilot, and the content pipeline behind my educational work. I publish the frameworks openly and use real builds to explain the decisions.

I build with Claude Code and Codex, work with Python and SQL, and have foundational TypeScript experience. I care about understanding the logic, making failure modes visible, and leaving a workflow people can maintain.
